extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers interested in the logic and methodology of scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proper use of deduction, induction, and hypotheses in scientific inquiry, including distinctions between derivative and ultimate laws and limits to explanation. Emphasizes testing, affiliation of special laws to more general laws, and cautions against both chimerical reductionism and unwarranted prohibition of explanatory attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method — premises must be experimentally established
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method should rest on premises established by legitimate canons of experimental inquiry, and its results must be tested by verification through specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deduce from premises 'hastily snatched up, or arbitrarily assumed' (the condemned Aristotelian style). Deduction regains primacy only when premisses have been legitimately induced and the deductions are verified by particular experiments or observations (i.e., deduction must be grounded and checked by induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of derivative laws into more general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws are observed uniformities that are deducible from other, more general laws; scientific progress consists in resolving special empirical regularities into simpler general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a general law is discovered, examine all cases presenting the necessary conditions for that law to act — this often yields demonstrations of previously unexplained special laws (examples: Dalton's atomic theory explaining chemical proportions; Graham's colloid/crystalloid distinction explaining osmose and digestion phenomena). Seeking affiliation of special results to broader principles both explains and suggests new cases to test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ultimate laws from derivative laws and respect limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate laws are those that cannot be further resolved into more general laws; derivative laws are resolvable. There must exist ultimate laws at least as numerous as distinguishable qualities of sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some aspects of phenomena (e.g., qualitative sensations like color) imply distinct ultimate laws that cannot be explained away by laws of different kinds. This sets a principled limit on the extent to which all phenomena can be reduced to a single law or a smaller set of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hypotheses as provisional explanatory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition made (without sufficient evidence) to deduce conclusions that accord with known facts; hypotheses are often introduced to explain phenomena when no known laws suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are legitimate initial devices for explanation. Their purpose is explanatory: to show how known facts might follow from assumed premises. However, being suppositions, they are provisional and must be capable of being subjected to further testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that hypotheses be submitted to inductive test
rubrics_metrics.description: To be accepted as truths rather than mere technical helps, hypotheses must be capable of being tested by the canons of legitimate induction and must actually be submitted to such tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An hypothesis may start as unproved, but it only becomes an accepted law when its deductive consequences are checked against experience. Therefore, always plan for empirical tests of any proposed hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of plausible hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Good hypotheses typically ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature; historically they are either (1) a real phenomenon whose law is supposed, or (2) a fictitious agency assumed to obey laws analogous to known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that are plausible (analogous to established phenomena) over wholly arbitrary inventions. Avoid assuming both an entirely fictitious agent and a wholly fictitious law; hypotheses gain plausibility and heuristic value when they relate to or extend familiar principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chimerical universal reductionism and also avoid premature prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Two errors to guard against: (a) the chimerical attempt to explain all phenomena by a single cause without empirical foundation, and (b) the dogmatic prohibition of reductionist attempts on the ground that some distinctions are 'primordial' and therefore unexplainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the legitimacy of attempting to reduce classes of phenomena when evidence suggests common antecedents (e.g., many motions explained by similar causes), while also respecting principled limits (distinct sensations may require distinct ultimate laws). Do not dismiss reductionist hypothesis outright because a phenomenon seems 'elementary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hypotheses that render phenomena representable and suggest tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are valuable insofar as they enable us to conceive obscure phenomena in familiar terms and to deduce consequences that can be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing hypotheses, choose formulations that make the phenomenon intelligible by analogy and that lead to observable, testable implications. The heuristic power to suggest new experiments or observable cases is a key criterion of a useful hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for new general laws when existing knowledge is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Many general laws of nature first appear as hypotheses that, if they deductively account for known concrete laws and survive inductive testing, will become accepted principia of a science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to proposing bold general hypotheses that might initially seem novel; ensure they are framed so their deductive consequences connect with known facts and are amenable to experimental or observational verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific experimental methods (e.g., Method of Difference) to establish causal links
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical methods such as the Method of Difference are essential to proving laws (examples: showing necessity of water to putrefaction by comparing dry and moist cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground claims about causes in carefully designed comparative experiments and observations. Employ the recognized methods of experimental inquiry to move from observed regularities to causal laws.
